summary: FireSight is a web application that summarizes, ranks and interprets NASA's microgravity combustion research to deliver fire-safety insights for human exploration. NASA's results are scattered across 24 PSI investigations, 176 technical reports and spreadsheets in different formats, so we built a Python pipeline that extracts, cleans and unifies them into one verified dataset of 622 tests, each traceable to its source and labeled as measured, extracted or estimated. On top of it, a validated model with uncertainty (AUC 0.86, 300 bootstrap refits) powers a habitat simulator, an atmosphere optimizer using NASA's crew-physiology limits, and an active-learning experiment designer. This directly answers the challenge: it identifies the investigations relevant to spacecraft, Moon bases, rovers and Mars habitats, exports data for predictive modeling, and highlights research for next-generation fire controls. It matters because Artemis-era habitats will breathe 30% oxygen at 10.2 psi, where flames persist far longer, and NASA's PSI data contains no microgravity tests of fabrics or plastics at those conditions.
details:
What it does and how it works

FireSight is a web application that turns NASA's scattered microgravity combustion research into decision-ready fire-safety answers for spacecraft, Moon bases, pressurized rovers, spacesuits and Mars habitats.

Data pipeline. A Python pipeline acquires the records of 24 investigations from NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) API, the PSI test tables (BASS, Saffire, ACME) and 176 NTRS reports. It extracts 275 FLEX tests that only existed as a table inside a PDF, unifies units and names, and fixes errors without ever inventing missing values. The result is 622 tests in one 25-field schema, each traceable to its source and labeled as measured, extracted or estimated.

Modeling. A logistic model of droplet-flame persistence, refit 300 times (bootstrap), gives every estimate a 90% interval. Leakage-free cross-validation gives AUC 0.86, against 0.81 for oxygen alone. Where the data could not support a model (ACME CFI-G), we show only measured statistics.

Tools.

Habitat Simulator: set any oxygen, pressure, gravity, ventilation and material.

Atmosphere Optimizer: 2,401 atmospheres × 300 models, checked against NASA's crew-physiology limits.

Experiment Designer: active learning over 1,092 candidate tests.

Saved scenarios: with side-by-side comparison and briefings.

Data gaps and materials maps.

Cited assistant: answers built from NASA passages.

Earth Mode.

Verification. An independent audit script recomputes every published number: 52 of 52 checks pass.

Benefits

One link, no account: scattered data becomes searchable, comparable and exportable (CSV/JSON, plus an open dataset and a notebook that reproduces the model).

Every result shows its uncertainty and how much measured evidence supports it, and missing data is flagged rather than guessed.

It goes beyond summaries: it supports decisions about habitat atmospheres and about which experiments to fly next.

Expected impact

For Artemis-era habitats planned at 30% oxygen and 10.2 psi, FireSight shows that droplet flames persist 97% of the time, against 66% on the ISS, and that gas flames last 5.5× longer.

It reveals that NASA's PSI data contains no microgravity tests of fabrics or plastics at those conditions, which makes that the top-priority experiment before crews live there.

Under NASA's own breathing and spacewalk limits, the optimizer lands on NASA's chosen 8.2 psi / 34% atmosphere and quantifies the fire risk that remains.

The same engine applies on Earth: airliner cabins, high-altitude cities, oxygen-enriched rooms and hyperbaric chambers.

Tools and technologies

Languages: Python and TypeScript.

Data and modeling: pandas, pypdf, scikit-learn, NumPy, SQLite (read-only).

Server: FastAPI and Uvicorn, packaged with Docker.

Interface: React, D3 and three.js (3D Earth from NASA Blue Marble), built with Vite; installable PWA that works offline.

Assistant: TF-IDF retrieval over 2,997 passages, plus an optional open-weight model (gpt-oss-20b via Groq's free API) that falls back to cited extracts.

Hosting (free, 24/7): GitHub, Render, cron-job.org.

No special hardware.

An AI coding assistant was used to write code under the team's direction. No data is AI-generated.

Creativity

Instead of only summarizing, FireSight couples fire data with crew physiology to find the best habitat atmosphere.

It uses active learning to plan NASA's next experiments.

Heavy calculations run live in the browser, with visible progress.

Every summary card recomputes for user-saved scenarios.

An independent mathematical audit is built in.

Factors the team considered

Scientific honesty: no invented data, explicit uncertainty, out-of-sample validation, and limits stated openly (no partial-gravity data exists in PSI, and the model covers droplet flames).

Accessibility: one link, mobile, offline, English, and three reading levels.

Zero cost: everything hosted on free tiers.

Security: a read-only database, input validation, a fixed path-traversal flaw, and rate limits on the AI assistant.

Data rights: raw PSI files are not redistributed.

No implied NASA endorsement.
